Why do zombie movies never call the zombies zombies, but every single vampire movie calls the vampires vampires?
I think in a lot of zombie movies the lore is that zombies never actually existed in pop culture before the walker/deady/rotter outbreak occurred.

Because in these stories vampires have existed for thousands of years and they even know how to kill them. In zombie movies it's always a brand new outbreak and zombies had never existed before. Think of how easy it would be to survive a zombie outbreak if you've seen one before and could prepare for it.
It couldn't be copyrighted because the word first appeared in English around 200 years ago.

My theory is the mythological/supernatural origin of vampires. They're a traditional folklore monster as opposed to a prosaic medical monster. Most zombie movies have nixed their voodoo origins in favor of the more popular virus angle. Because of this, you have to make it believable and grounded that a virus can animate the dead in a global catastrophe, which leads to operating with the premise that folks would be in denial until it's too late to do anything.

Vampires on the other hand are ubiquitous in their fantasy nature. It's much harder to believe in a supernatural god-fearing demon than a viris turned walker. They're pure fantasy and allowed to existed in the idiom without their universe being "confused" as a part of the gimmick.

It's because those movies require a "crisis". So the "monster" has to be dangerous, in the case of zombies generally so dangerous they destroy human civilization.

With zombies the danger of spread and difficulty fighting zombies relies on the general populace not being familiar with head shots and avoiding contamination.

In contrast a super strong, super fast vampire who has a variety of "magic" abilities is still pretty damn tough even if you're completely prepared for them.
